overview: Two of the three muscle types, differing in voluntary control, appearance under a microscope, and where they're found in the body.
genZNote: Skeletal muscle: the one you consciously flex. Smooth muscle: the one working quietly in your organs without you ever thinking about it.

aspects.label: Microscopic Appearance
aspects.valueA: Striated (banded) appearance, with multiple nuclei per cell.
aspects.valueB: Non-striated (smooth) appearance, with a single central nucleus per cell.

aspects.label: Typical Location
aspects.valueA: Attached to bones, enabling body movement.
aspects.valueB: Found in the walls of internal organs like the stomach, intestines, and blood vessels.

aspects.label: Fatigue Resistance
aspects.valueA: Fatigues relatively quickly with sustained use.
aspects.valueB: Fatigues slowly, suited for prolonged, sustained contraction.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Skeletal muscle's striations come from the highly organised arrangement of actin and myosin filaments, visible clearly under a microscope — a classic ID question.
overlay.memoryTrick: Skeletal = striated and voluntary, attached to bone. Smooth = non-striated and involuntary, in organ walls.
overlay.commonMisconception: Smooth muscle is not 'weaker' just because it's involuntary — it's simply built for sustained, low-fatigue contraction rather than powerful, quick movements.
